newsitem.title: USA: No new talks in UPS strike; other firms cutting jobs.
newsitem.headline: No new talks in UPS strike; other firms cutting jobs.

text.p: The Clinton administration tried to revive talks between United Parcel Service and the striking Teamsters Wednesday, but neither side budged and other companies laid off workers because of the walkout.

The impact of the 10-day-old strike spread as Russ Berrie and Co. Inc., a New Jersey-based maker of plush dolls and gift items, and National TechTeam Inc., which provides technical services to UPS customers, each said they cut about 100 workers.

"At this time of year, we're shipping a lot of seasonal and Christmas items. We can't find enough sources to get out the products," Russ Berrie President Curts Cooke said, adding the company's shipments were about 25 percent of normal.

National TechTeam, based in Dearborn, Mich., said it laid off about 100 employees who worked with a 175-member team that provides technical support to customers tied to UPS's computer system. Chief Executive William Coyro said the company would place the workers in temporary slots on other projects until the UPS strike ends.
UPS Chairman James Kelly said efforts to end the strike by 185,000 Teamsters were at an impasse, even as Labor Secretary Alexis Herman tried to get talks restarted.
Depsite signs that the strike's impact was widening, White House spokesman Mike McCurry gave no sign that President Bill Clinton would change his mind and step in.

"As a general premise, we take the view that government should not step in and resolve labor-management disputes, that they ought to be resolved by the parties through collective bargaining," McCurry said during his daily briefing.

As the two sides dug in, the Independent Pilots Association of UPS pilots -- which has refused to cross Teamster picket lines to fly 500 UPS planes -- issued a warning to pilots whose airlines were carrying UPS packages.
"Effective on Friday, Aug. 15 ... all flights carrying struck UPS goods will be considered strike-breaking activity," the union said. It scheduled a news conference for Thursday.
On Tuesday, the AFL-CIO offered millions of dollars to help the Teamsters pay strike benefits to people on picket lines, while UPS warned it will cut 15,000 jobs because of lost business.
UPS took out national newspaper ads Tuesday to tell its side of the story, but a poll showed the Teamsters winning the battle for public opinion.

The ABC News poll released late Tuesday showed 40 percent of Americans backed the union in its fight to win more higher-paying, full-time jobs. UPS won 30 percent support in the survey of 506 adults conducted on Monday, while 30 percent said they were neutral.
"I don't know if I can convince Americans," UPS' Kelly said in an interview with CNN in response to the poll. "What I'm trying to do is convince UPS people."

The poll also showed support for Clinton's position, indicating 64 percent of those polled opposed presidential intervention in the strike. To intervene, Clinton would have to seek a court order under the Taft-Hartley law, last used by President Jimmy Carter in 1978.

Carter intervened when a coal miners strike dragged on for three months and won a court order that was largely ignored. Carter lost in court on March 17, 1978, when a federal judge refused to extend the order, citing the absence of "evidence of irreparable harm to the national health or safety."
Given that history, the administration limited itself to talking.
"Labor Secretary Alexis Herman continued to talk to both parties by telephone well into the night and morning to get both parties back to negotiating table," a spokesman said.
But Kelly said he saw no prospect of a quick settlement and said negotiations were going nowhere.
"I would characterize them as being at an impasse," he said on CNN. He insisted, as he has before, that the union should allow members to vote on the company's last offer.
UPS normally handles 12 million packages a day, 80 percent of them shipped by ground nationwide, and many businesses have struggled to deliver goods or find alternate shippers.
